title: Inquest rules shooting death a homicide
article: The death of Kevin Edmond St. Arnaud was a homicide by an RCMP officer in the line of duty, a coroner's jury determined Friday.
St. Arnaud died from gunshot wounds to the chest at 1:09 a.m. on Dec. 19, 2004, at the soccer fields off Stewart Street in Vanderhoof, the three-woman, two-man jury concluded.

On the afternoon of Dec. 18, 2004, St. Arnaud, a welder, injured his hand at work, went to St. John Hospital for treatment, returned to work but then went home early. That evening he went to the pub with his girlfriend and at first was very happy and the life of the party. Later, his mood declined and late in the evening, he walked to a home in a state of considerable intoxication, court heard. His blood-alcohol level was more than twice the legal limit for drivers.

An alarm went off at the Rexall pharmacy at the Co-Op Mall on Dec. 19, 2004, at 12:51 a.m. Two officers responded. A man identified as St. Arnaud had gone through the roof to get into the dispensary and then run out the door of a restaurant in the mall. Const. Ryan Sherematta followed him in a police vehicle and then on foot to the soccer fields. He said he fired three shots after St. Arnaud stopped running and turned toward him aggressively. Evidence heard Friday continued to reflect discrepancies in testimony from witnesses as to whether Sherematta fired after having fallen backward or was standing in a full combat stance when he discharged the three fatal shots.
The coroner's inquest lasted six days. After deliberating for more than an hour and a half, the three-woman, two-man jury made seven recommendations to help prevent such incidents in future.

One was to the Vanderhoof RCMP to consider changes to staffing levels on weekends, evenings and holidays. Another was to improve communications between officers involved in investigating incidents and "ensure officers involved in investigating incidents properly identify themselves, including using emergency lights where appropriate."

On Friday afternoon, just before the jury prepared to go out for its deliberations, Dolores Young, St. Arnaud's mother, forwarded recommendations to Chief Coroner Shane DeMeyer for the jurors' consideration. DeMeyer said he could not provide them to the jurors, but would enter them as an exhibit.

Outside the courtroom, Young said she had three recommendations. One was that the time involved in the process should not be so long. "It's been more than two years, and that seems excessive," she said.
"Secondly, the RCMP should not investigate themselves in cases of serious harm or death where a member is involved," Young said.

Third, given that the services of coroner's counsel and counsel for the RCMP are paid for by the taxpayers, family members of the deceased should have publicly-funded legal representation at coroner's inquests, she said.
Other recommendations from the jury were that the B.C. Liquor Distribution Branch review and ensure proper enforcement regarding sales of alcohol in licensed premises.
Jurors also called on the owners and managers of the Co-Op Mall to ensure that all potential access sites on the roof be secured.
The jury's recommendation to the Prince George RCMP operations and communications centre was that personnel "ensure as much detail as possible be provided to officers upon report of an alarm."
